document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use presents with a three-day history of fever, rigors, and pleuritic chest pain. He is coughing up thick, blood-tinged sputum that the nurse describes as resembling red currant jelly. Chest x-ray shows a dense right upper lobe consolidation with early cavitation. Which organism is the most likely cause of his pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists Klebsiella first among the organisms causing pneumonia in patients with alcohol use disorder, and notes the classic association 'when Klebsiella causes pneumonia: see red currant jelly sputum'. This patient's alcohol use disorder combined with thick blood-tinged sputum and a cavitating upper lobe consolidation fits that pattern.

optionExplanations.b: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an atypical community-acquired organism and is not among those listed for alcohol use disorder or for red currant jelly sputum.
optionExplanations.c: Moraxella catarrhalis is a typical community-acquired pathogen but is not associated with alcohol use disorder or cavitary disease in this table.
optionExplanations.d: Legionella pneumophila is listed as an atypical community-acquired pathogen, not as a characteristic organism in alcohol use disorder.
optionExplanations.e: Chlamydia pneumoniae is an atypical community-acquired pathogen and does not produce the described sputum or cavitation.

source.reference: ID7 — Pneumonia: Common Organisms in Pneumonia

questions.question: A 79-year-old woman presents with a two-day history of cough and fever. She is disoriented to time and place. Her respiratory rate is 34 breaths/min, blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg, and temperature is 38.6 C. Serum urea is 11.2 mmol/L. Chest x-ray confirms a left lower lobe consolidation consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. Based on her CURB-65 score, which disposition is most appropriate?

options.text: Discharge home with oral antibiotics and telephone follow-up in 48 hours
Discharge home with community nursing visits and outpatient review
Observe in the emergency department for 12 hours and then reassess
Admit to a general medical ward
Admit to an intensive care unit

questions.explanation: The CURB-65 tool assigns one point each for Confusion, Urea 7 mmol/L or greater, Respiratory rate 30 breaths/min or greater, systolic BP under 90 mmHg or diastolic 60 mmHg or lower, and Age 65 or older. This patient meets all five criteria, giving a score of 5. Toronto Notes places scores of 4-5 in the 15-30% mortality band, for which the recommended disposition is to consider ICU care.

optionExplanations.a: Outpatient treatment is recommended only for a CURB-65 score of 0-1, which corresponds to under 5% mortality.
optionExplanations.b: Home-based care still falls in the outpatient category and is reserved for scores of 0-1.
optionExplanations.c: Brief observation does not address the 15-30% predicted mortality associated with a score of 4-5.
optionExplanations.d: Ward admission corresponds to a score of 2-3 (5-15% mortality); a score of 4-5 warrants consideration of ICU care.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with COPD and type 2 diabetes attends his family physician with four days of productive cough, fever, and pleuritic chest pain. Chest x-ray shows a right middle lobe infiltrate. He is alert and normotensive with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. He has never had MRSA or Pseudomonas isolated and has not been hospitalised recently. Which is the best initial outpatient antimicrobial regimen?
questions.explanation: The 2019 IDSA/ATS community-acquired pneumonia guideline reproduced in Toronto Notes divides outpatients by comorbidity. For outpatients with comorbidities such as chronic lung disease or diabetes, the recommended empiric therapy is amoxicillin/clavulanate or a cephalosporin PLUS a macrolide or doxycycline, or alternatively a respiratory fluoroquinolone. This man has both COPD and diabetes, so combination therapy is indicated.

optionExplanations.a: Amoxicillin monotherapy is recommended only for outpatients with no comorbidities and no MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors.
optionExplanations.b: Macrolide monotherapy is an option only for outpatients without comorbidities, and only where local pneumococcal resistance is under 25%.
optionExplanations.d: Ciprofloxacin is not one of the respiratory fluoroquinolones listed; the guideline specifies moxifloxacin or levofloxacin.
optionExplanations.e: Cephalexin is not a listed community-acquired pneumonia agent, and a cephalosporin would still need to be combined with a macrolide or doxycycline.

source.reference: ID8 — Table 11. IDSA/ATS Community-Acquired Pneumonia Treatment Guidelines 2019

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant presents in January with a 20-hour history of abrupt fever, chills, myalgias, headache, and dry cough. Influenza A is circulating widely in the community and a nasopharyngeal swab has been sent for RT-PCR. She appears unwell but her chest examination and chest x-ray are normal and her oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Which is the best initial antiviral therapy?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that influenza treatment is primarily supportive unless the infection is severe or the patient is at high risk of complications, and lists pregnancy among the high-risk groups. The neuraminidase inhibitor oseltamivir decreases duration by about one day and reduces severity when given within 48 hours of symptom onset, which applies here at 20 hours.

optionExplanations.b: Acyclovir covers HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV, and has no activity against influenza viruses.
optionExplanations.c: Remdesivir is listed for COVID-19, not for influenza.
optionExplanations.d: Ribavirin is listed for chronic hepatitis C, RSV, and Lassa fever, and is highly teratogenic, making it inappropriate in pregnancy.
optionExplanations.e: Valganciclovir targets CMV and other herpesviruses, not influenza.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man is on day 9 of a hospital admission for cellulitis treated with clindamycin. He develops six episodes of watery diarrhoea per day, lower abdominal cramping, nausea, and a low-grade fever. His white blood cell count has risen to 18.2 x 10^9/L. His abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness and no distension. Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Stool PCR for toxin A and B genes
Stool immunoassay for toxins A and B
Blood cultures from two peripheral sites

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists stool PCR for the toxin A and B genes as the investigation for Clostridioides difficile infection, and explicitly notes that the stool immunoassay for toxins A and B is less sensitive than PCR. Antibiotic exposure (clindamycin is specifically named as a culprit), watery diarrhoea, fever, abdominal pain, and leukocytosis are the classic manifestations.

optionExplanations.b: The stool immunoassay for toxins A and B is described as less sensitive than PCR and is therefore not the preferred first test.
optionExplanations.c: Abdominal x-ray is used to look for colonic dilatation in severe disease, not to establish the diagnosis.
optionExplanations.d: Sigmoidoscopy for pseudomembranes is an adjunct and should be avoided if colonic dilatation is known.
optionExplanations.e: Blood cultures do not detect C. difficile, which causes disease through exotoxins released in the colon.

source.reference: ID6 — Table 7. Common Nosocomial Infectious Agents

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman hospitalised for a urinary tract infection treated with ciprofloxacin develops profuse watery diarrhoea, fever, and abdominal pain on day 7. Stool PCR is positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin A and B genes. She has no ileus, no abdominal distension, and a normal blood pressure. The ciprofloxacin has been stopped, intravenous fluids started, and contact precautions instituted. Which is the best initial antimicrobial therapy?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that management of C. difficile infection includes stopping the culprit antibiotic, supportive IV fluids, and empiric treatment with either vancomycin or fidaxomicin, with metronidazole used only if access to empiric treatment is limited. Vancomycin is effective against C. difficile when given orally, so oral vancomycin is the appropriate choice here.

optionExplanations.b: Vancomycin acts on C. difficile within the colonic lumen; the oral route is what is used for this indication.
optionExplanations.c: Metronidazole is a fallback when access to first-line empiric treatment is limited, and IV metronidazole is reserved for fulminant infection with ileus, which she does not have.
optionExplanations.d: Amoxicillin has no role and further antibiotic pressure would worsen the infection.
optionExplanations.e: Ceftriaxone does not treat C. difficile and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure is a precipitant of the disease.

source.reference: ID6 — Table 7. Common Nosocomial Infectious Agents

questions.question: A 52-year-old man presents with a two-day history of a painful, warm, red, swollen left lower leg with indistinct borders and visible red streaking extending toward the knee. He is febrile at 38.4 C. There is no fluctuance, no abscess, and no drainage. Examination of his feet reveals scaling and fissuring between the toes consistent with tinea pedis. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes identifies beta-hemolytic streptococci as the most common cause of non-purulent cellulitis, with S. aureus and occasionally S. lugdunensis also implicated. Cracked skin of the feet from tinea pedis is listed as a risk factor, and ascending lymphangitis producing visible red streaking is a recognised feature. The absence of pus points away from a purulent, staphylococcal process.

optionExplanations.b: Gram-negative rods such as Pseudomonas are considered in immunocompromised patients or after water exposure, neither of which applies.
optionExplanations.c: Anaerobes such as Bacteroides are not listed among common causative agents of simple cellulitis.
optionExplanations.d: Enteric Gram-negative organisms are not typical causes of non-purulent cellulitis in an immunocompetent host.
optionExplanations.e: C. difficile causes colitis through exotoxins and does not cause skin and soft tissue infection.

source.reference: ID11 — Skin and Soft Tissue Infections: Cellulitis

questions.question: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a plantar forefoot ulcer with surrounding redness, warmth, and tenderness extending about 1 cm beyond the ulcer margin. There is no pus, no crepitus, and a sterile probe does not reach bone. He is afebrile with normal vital signs, a normal white blood cell count, and an unremarkable plain x-ray. Which is the best initial empiric antimicrobial therapy?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies a diabetic foot infection as mild when it is superficial with no bone or joint involvement, moderate when it is deep or erythema extends more than 2 cm, and severe when there is systemic toxicity. This ulcer is superficial with only about 1 cm of erythema and no systemic features, so it is mild, and the recommended empiric treatment is cloxacillin or cephalexin, later adjusted by culture and response.

optionExplanations.b: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the recommended empiric choice for moderate or severe infection, not for a mild superficial infection.
optionExplanations.c: Ceftriaxone is likewise reserved for moderate or severe diabetic foot infection.
optionExplanations.d: Piperacillin-tazobactam is a broad-spectrum agent not listed for diabetic foot infection at this severity.
optionExplanations.e: Combination broad Gram-positive and anaerobic coverage exceeds what is recommended for a mild superficial infection.

source.reference: ID15 — Diabetic Foot Infections: Infection Severity and Treatment

questions.question: A 31-year-old man who injects drugs presents with a two-week history of fever, rigors, and pleuritic chest pain. His temperature is 39.1 C. A soft systolic murmur is audible at the left lower sternal border and increases with inspiration. Chest x-ray shows multiple peripheral nodular opacities, several of which are cavitating. He has no prosthetic material and three sets of blood cultures have been drawn. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes shows that in injection drug use-associated infective endocarditis S. aureus is by far the leading pathogen at 68%, followed by Streptococcus at 13%. It also notes that the tricuspid valve is involved in 50% of IVDU-related cases, which fits a murmur that increases with inspiration and septic pulmonary emboli seen as cavitating nodules.

optionExplanations.b: Streptococcus accounts for about 13% of IVDU endocarditis and predominates instead in native valve disease at 36%.
optionExplanations.c: Enterococcus is listed as a less frequent pathogen in this setting, well behind S. aureus.
optionExplanations.d: S. epidermidis is characteristically associated with prosthetic valve endocarditis, and he has no prosthetic material.
optionExplanations.e: Candida is listed as an uncommon IVDU pathogen and would be unusual as the first consideration here.

source.reference: ID15 — Table 17. Microbial Etiology of Infective Endocarditis Based on Risk Factors

questions.question: A 67-year-old woman who had a bioprosthetic aortic valve inserted three years ago presents with six weeks of fever, weight loss, and night sweats. Three sets of blood cultures drawn more than one hour apart all grow Staphylococcus epidermidis. A transthoracic echocardiogram is technically limited by body habitus and shows no vegetation, but the clinical suspicion for infective endocarditis remains high. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat transthoracic echocardiography in one week
Serum rheumatoid factor and erythrocyte sedimentation rate

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that transthoracic echocardiography has poor sensitivity and is inadequate in about 20% of patients because of obesity, COPD, or chest wall deformities, and that transesophageal echocardiography is indicated when TTE is non-diagnostic in a patient with at least possible endocarditis, when prosthetic valve endocarditis is suspected, or when complicated endocarditis is suspected. TEE has roughly 90% sensitivity.

optionExplanations.b: Repeating a study that was technically inadequate will not overcome the limitation that made it non-diagnostic.
optionExplanations.c: Chest x-ray does not image valvular vegetations or perivalvular complications.
optionExplanations.d: Rheumatoid factor and ESR are supportive bloodwork in endocarditis but do not demonstrate valvular involvement.
optionExplanations.e: Urinalysis may show proteinuria or hematuria but does not confirm or exclude endocarditis.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and increasing confusion. Lumbar puncture yields turbid fluid with 3200 leukocytes/microL of which 92% are neutrophils, glucose 1.4 mmol/L, and protein 3.8 g/L. Gram stain of the cerebrospinal fluid shows Gram-positive rods. Which organism is the most likely cause of his meningitis?
questions.explanation: The CSF profile of markedly raised protein, low glucose, and a neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis indicates bacterial meningitis. Toronto Notes lists L. monocytogenes as Gram-positive rods on CSF Gram stain and notes it is a likely pathogen in patients over 50 or with comorbidities, which matches this 72-year-old man.

optionExplanations.b: S. pneumoniae appears as Gram-positive diplococci, not rods.
optionExplanations.c: N. meningitidis appears as Gram-negative diplococci.
optionExplanations.d: H. influenzae appears as pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli.
optionExplanations.e: Group B Streptococcus is listed as a neonatal and young infant pathogen and is a coccus, not a rod.

source.reference: ID17 — Meningitis: Table 19 Common Organisms and CSF Gram Stain Findings

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with a long-standing alcohol use disorder is brought in with fever, headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness that began this morning. He is drowsy but has no focal neurological deficit and no papilloedema. Blood cultures are drawn and lumbar puncture performed immediately; the cerebrospinal fluid is turbid and the Gram stain result is pending. Which is the best initial empiric antimicrobial regimen?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes gives empiric therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis in patients over 3 months of age as ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, and specifies adding IV ampicillin when risk factors for Listeria monocytogenes are present, namely age over 50, alcohol use disorder, or immunocompromise. This patient has an alcohol use disorder, so ampicillin must be added.

optionExplanations.a: Ceftriaxone monotherapy omits vancomycin for resistant pneumococcus and ampicillin for Listeria.
optionExplanations.b: This is the standard regimen for patients over 3 months without Listeria risk factors, but his alcohol use disorder requires added ampicillin.
optionExplanations.d: Ampicillin plus cefotaxime is the regimen recommended for neonates under 28 days of age.
optionExplanations.e: Vancomycin plus gentamicin is an endocarditis regimen and provides inadequate CNS coverage of the expected meningitis pathogens.

questions.question: A 36-year-old woman awoke to find a bat flying in her bedroom and has a small puncture wound on her forearm. The bat escaped and is unavailable for testing. She has never received rabies vaccine. The exposure has been reported to the local public health authority, and she is otherwise well with a clean-appearing wound and no systemic symptoms. Which is the most appropriate post-exposure management?

options.text: Thorough wound cleansing, rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound site, and rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, and 14
Thorough wound cleansing and rabies vaccine on days 0 and 3 only
Thorough wound cleansing and rabies immunoglobulin alone
Thorough wound cleansing and rabies vaccine given into the gluteal muscle without immunoglobulin
Thorough wound cleansing and observation, reserving prophylaxis until symptoms develop

questions.explanation: For a person not previously immunised, Toronto Notes specifies cleaning the wound promptly and thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes, passive immunisation with rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound site with any remaining volume given IM at a distant site, and active immunisation with human diploid cell rabies vaccine as a series of four doses on days 0, 3, 7, and 14.

optionExplanations.b: The two-dose day 0 and day 3 schedule without immunoglobulin applies only to people who were previously immunised.
optionExplanations.c: Immunoglobulin alone omits active immunisation, which is part of the recommended regimen in unimmunised people.
optionExplanations.d: Because of variable response rates the vaccine should be given into the deltoid rather than the gluteal muscle, and immunoglobulin is required in unimmunised people.
optionExplanations.e: Once prodromal symptoms develop there is rapid, irreversible progression to death, and treatment is only supportive at that point.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man presents in July, ten days after a camping trip in southeastern Ontario. He reports fatigue, headache, and myalgias. Examination reveals a 9 cm expanding, non-pruritic, erythematous annular lesion with central clearing on his posterior thigh. He is afebrile, with no cranial nerve palsy, no joint swelling, and a normal cardiac examination. Which is the best initial antimicrobial therapy?
questions.explanation: Erythema migrans, an expanding non-pruritic bulls-eye lesion appearing 7-14 days after a tick bite, defines stage 1 early localised Lyme disease, which Toronto Notes notes is primarily a clinical diagnosis because serology may be negative at this stage. Treatment of stage 1 is doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime.

optionExplanations.b: Ceftriaxone is listed for stage 2 and stage 3 disease, and he has no neurologic, cardiac, or arthritic involvement.
optionExplanations.c: Azithromycin is not among the agents listed for any stage of Lyme disease.
optionExplanations.d: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is not a listed treatment for Lyme disease.
optionExplanations.e: Ciprofloxacin is not a listed treatment for Lyme disease.

source.reference: ID22 — Lyme Disease: Clinical Features and Treatment

questions.question: A 26-year-old man presents with a solitary, painless, indurated ulcer on the penile shaft that appeared ten days ago, together with non-tender bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. He has no rash, fever, or neurological symptoms. Public health laboratory testing confirms syphilis. He has no drug allergies and no evidence of tertiary or neurological disease. Which is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for three weeks
Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 14 days
Aqueous penicillin G 16-24 million units per day IV for 14 days

questions.explanation: A painless chancre at the inoculation site with regional lymphadenopathy 3-90 days after infection defines primary syphilis. Toronto Notes gives the treatment for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis as benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once. He has no penicillin allergy, so first-line therapy applies.

optionExplanations.b: Three weekly doses are reserved for tertiary and late latent syphilis, where a longer treatment duration is required.
optionExplanations.c: Doxycycline for 14 days is second-line therapy only for patients who are truly penicillin-allergic.
optionExplanations.d: High-dose IV aqueous penicillin G for 14 days is the neurosyphilis regimen, and he has no neurological features.
optionExplanations.e: A 10-day IV penicillin G course is the regimen specified for congenital syphilis.

questions.question: A 43-year-old man who immigrated from a country with high tuberculosis prevalence presents with three months of productive cough, night sweats, and 8 kg of weight loss. Chest x-ray shows a right apical cavitary infiltrate. Three sputum specimens are smear-positive for acid-fast bacilli and culture later confirms fully susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He is HIV-negative, is not pregnant-capable, and has normal liver enzymes. Which is the best initial treatment regimen?

options.text: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months
Isoniazid with pyridoxine daily for 9 months
Isoniazid with pyridoxine plus rifapentine weekly for 3 months

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes specifies that pulmonary tuberculosis disease is treated with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for a 2-month initiation phase, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months in fully susceptible disease, for a total of 6 months. The continuation phase is extended to 7 months only if the patient is over 65, pregnant, or at risk of hepatotoxicity.

optionExplanations.b: Two-drug therapy from the outset omits the four-drug initiation phase required for active disease and risks resistance.
optionExplanations.c: Rifampin daily for 4 months is a regimen for preventing reactivation of latent infection, and active disease must be ruled out before using it.
optionExplanations.d: Isoniazid with pyridoxine for 9 months is a latent tuberculosis infection regimen, not treatment of active disease.
optionExplanations.e: Weekly isoniazid, pyridoxine, and rifapentine for 3 months is also a latent tuberculosis infection regimen.

source.reference: ID26 — Tuberculosis: Prevention and Treatment of TB Disease

questions.question: A 38-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV and is currently asymptomatic. His baseline CD4 count is 140 cells/mm3 and HIV RNA is 85,000 copies/mL. Toxoplasma IgG is negative, tuberculin skin test induration measures 0 mm with no known contact with active tuberculosis, and he has had no opportunistic infection. Antiretroviral therapy is being arranged. Which prophylactic regimen is most appropriate to start now?

options.text: Isoniazid with pyridoxine daily for 9 months

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii as indicated when the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/mm3, with TMP/SMX single or double strength once daily as the preferred regimen. His CD4 count of 140 crosses that threshold, whereas the thresholds and indications for the other listed prophylaxes are not met.

optionExplanations.b: Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis is considered at a CD4 count under 50 cells/mm3, and no prophylaxis is needed if patients are started on antiretroviral therapy.
optionExplanations.c: Isoniazid with pyridoxine is indicated for a PPD reaction of 5 mm or greater or contact with a case of active tuberculosis, neither of which is present.
optionExplanations.d: Fluconazole is not listed as routine primary prophylaxis in the opportunistic infection prophylaxis table.
optionExplanations.e: Valganciclovir targets CMV, which becomes a concern at CD4 counts under 50 cells/mm3, and it is not listed as routine prophylaxis.

source.reference: ID29 — Table 23. Prophylaxis Against Opportunistic Infections in HIV-infected Patients

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman returns from a two-week holiday at urban Caribbean resorts and presents five days later with abrupt high fever, severe frontal and retro-orbital headache, marked myalgias and arthralgias, and a diffuse rash. She recalls daytime mosquito bites and took no antimalarial prophylaxis. Bloodwork shows leukopenia and a platelet count of 88 x 10^9/L. There is no jaundice, eschar, or splenomegaly. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes dengue as occurring in Southeast Asia and the Caribbean, usually transmitted by urban day-biting mosquitoes, with an incubation period of 3 days to 2 weeks and sudden onset of fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgias, and arthralgias accompanied by leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Her exposure, timing, and laboratory findings match this profile.

optionExplanations.b: Malaria is listed for Africa, India, Central and South America, and Southeast Asia, typically with rural night-biting mosquitoes, and characteristically produces anemia and jaundice rather than retro-orbital pain.
optionExplanations.c: Typhoid produces a sustained fever of 39-40 C with abdominal pain, constipation, and positive stool, urine, or blood cultures, not an abrupt retro-orbital headache syndrome.
optionExplanations.d: Tick typhus occurs in the Mediterranean, South Africa, and India and features an eschar at the tick bite site with elevated liver enzymes.
optionExplanations.e: Mononucleosis has a 30-50 day incubation with malaise, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, none of which fits this 5-day presentation.

source.reference: ID43 — Table 30. Fever in the Returned Traveller

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis presents with two days of a painful, swollen, warm right knee. He is unable to weight bear and has a markedly decreased range of motion. Temperature is 38.4degC. There is no history of trauma or prior joint surgery. Plain x-ray of the knee shows no bony destruction. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count and differential, Gram stain, culture and sensitivity, and assessment for crystals
Blood cultures alone with observation for 24 hours
Empiric oral antibiotics with outpatient follow-up in one week

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that in suspected septic arthritis arthrocentesis is mandatory, and that synovial fluid analysis should include CBC and differential, Gram stain, C&S, and assessment for crystals; infectious fluid is opaque with increased WBCs, PMNs greater than 90%, and positive culture. Underlying joint disease such as rheumatoid arthritis is a listed risk factor for non-gonococcal septic arthritis, and delay in diagnosis and treatment may result in joint destruction.

optionExplanations.b: Intra-articular steroids are contraindicated until septic arthritis has been excluded.
optionExplanations.c: MRI is not the initial test; plain x-ray is used to assess for osteomyelitis and provide a baseline, and joint fluid is still required.
optionExplanations.d: Blood C&S is recommended but does not replace the mandatory arthrocentesis, and observation risks joint destruction.
optionExplanations.e: Empiric therapy in septic arthritis is with IV antibiotics after joint fluid is obtained, not oral outpatient therapy.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man on hemodialysis through a tunnelled central venous catheter presents with fever, rigors, and confusion. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci. After 48 hours of piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin he remains febrile with persistently positive blood cultures. He is now normotensive off vasopressors, and no other focus of infection is identified. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Remove the infected central venous catheter
Add an aminoglycoside for drug-resistant Gram-negatives
Continue the same antibiotics and repeat blood cultures in a further 48 hours
Narrow therapy to a single agent based on susceptibilities

questions.explanation: Treatment of sepsis includes source control, defined in Toronto Notes as a procedure to control the focus of infection such as catheter removal or abscess drainage, alongside respiratory support, cardiovascular support, and empiric IV antibiotics. This man has persistent bacteremia on appropriate broad-spectrum coverage with an indwelling catheter as the only identified focus, so antibiotics alone will not clear the infection.

optionExplanations.b: An aminoglycoside is added for suspected drug-resistant Gram-negatives; his cultures grow Gram-positive cocci already covered by vancomycin.
optionExplanations.c: IV hydrocortisone is reserved for septic shock unresponsive to fluid resuscitation and vasopressors, and he is now normotensive off vasopressors.
optionExplanations.d: Waiting does not address the focus of infection and allows ongoing bacteremia.
optionExplanations.e: Narrowing once the organism and susceptibilities are known is appropriate eventually, but it does not control the source.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man presents with five days of fever, pharyngitis, myalgias, arthralgias, and a diffuse rash. He has generalized lymphadenopathy and shallow oral ulcers. Three weeks earlier he had condomless sex with a new partner. Bloodwork shows lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia. A third-generation HIV antibody ELISA is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that 40-90% of people with new HIV infection experience an acute non-specific illness 2-6 wk post-exposure lasting 10-15 d, which may include fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, rash, arthralgias, myalgias, headache, GI symptoms, and oral ulcers, with hematologic disturbances such as lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia. Anti-HIV antibodies are detectable only after a median of 3 wk, so a negative antibody screen during this window period does not exclude infection; this stage carries a high level of plasma viremia and high risk of transmission.

optionExplanations.b: EBV is associated with mononucleosis and oral hairy leukoplakia, but does not explain the recent high-risk sexual exposure with a negative antibody screen in the window period.
optionExplanations.c: CMV disease in Toronto Notes is described at CD4 counts under 50 cells/mm3, presenting as retinitis, colitis, cholangiopathy, or CNS disease.
optionExplanations.d: Primary VZV causes chicken pox with a vesicular rash, not oral ulcers with lymphopenia after a sexual exposure.
optionExplanations.e: MAC is a late opportunistic infection occurring at CD4 counts under 50 cells/mm3, not a seroconversion illness.

questions.question: A 33-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV and is treatment-naive and asymptomatic. Baseline investigations show a CD4 count of 410 cells/mm3, an HIV viral load of 45,000 copies/mL, normal renal and hepatic function, and a positive HLA-B*5701 result. He is not of childbearing potential. Which is the most appropriate initial antiretroviral regimen?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists bictegravir/TAF/FTC first among recommended regimens for treatment-naive adults, noting that most initial regimens include an integrase strand transfer inhibitor and a pair of NRTIs. Dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine is recommended only in patients confirmed to be HLA-B*5701 negative, because abacavir causes drug-induced hypersensitivity; this man is HLA-B*5701 positive, so any abacavir-containing regimen must be avoided.

optionExplanations.b: This single tablet regimen is to be used only in HLA-B*5701 negative patients because it contains abacavir.
optionExplanations.c: It contains abacavir, and efavirenz-based regimens are associated with psychiatric events and vivid dreams rather than being first line.
optionExplanations.d: This combination tablet also contains abacavir, and zidovudine adds bone marrow suppression and myopathy.
optionExplanations.e: Protease inhibitor-based therapy is not among the recommended initial regimens and carries lipodystrophy, metabolic syndrome, and CYP3A4 interactions.

questions.question: A 27-year-old healthcare worker sustains a deep needle-stick injury while drawing blood from a patient known to be HIV positive. She is otherwise well and takes no medications. She presents to occupational health two hours after the exposure, and baseline HIV serology is drawn. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Start a 2- or 3-drug antiretroviral regimen immediately and continue it for 4 weeks
Start daily tenofovir/emtricitabine as ongoing pre-exposure prophylaxis
Give a double dose of antiretrovirals now, then single doses at 24 and 48 hours
Withhold antiretrovirals and repeat HIV serology in 3 months
Give antiretrovirals only if the source patient is found not to be virally suppressed on ART

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that post-exposure prophylaxis after occupational exposure to HIV, such as a needle-stick injury, is a 2- or 3-drug regimen initiated immediately (less than 72 h after exposure) and continued for 4 wk. Universal blood and body precautions plus prompt PEP are the mainstays of preventing occupationally acquired HIV, and prophylaxis should not be delayed while further information is gathered.

optionExplanations.b: Daily TDF/FTC is a pre-exposure prophylaxis strategy for people at ongoing risk, not the response to a discrete exposure that has already occurred.
optionExplanations.c: Double dosing 12-24 h before exposure followed by doses at 24 and 48 h is the 2-1-1 on-demand PrEP schedule, which is taken around anticipated exposure.
optionExplanations.d: Deferring therapy forfeits the narrow window in which PEP must be started.
optionExplanations.e: PEP is started immediately after a significant exposure; waiting on source testing risks exceeding the 72 h window.

questions.question: A 47-year-old man who lives in Northern Ontario presents with three months of cough, chest pain, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. He has several verrucous skin lesions on his forearm that mimic skin cancer. Chest x-ray shows a lobar pneumonia. Direct examination of purulent sputum shows broad-based budding yeast. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes Blastomyces dermatitidis as endemic to states east of the Mississippi River, Northern Ontario, and along the Great Lakes, presenting with acute or chronic pneumonia with fever, cough, chest pain, chills, night sweats, and weight loss, and disseminating to skin as verrucous lesions that mimic skin cancer. Diagnosis is by direct examination of clinical specimens for characteristic broad-based budding yeast in sputum, tissue, or purulent material.

optionExplanations.b: Histoplasmosis is endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys and is diagnosed by antigen detection in urine and serum; disseminated disease occurs primarily in immunocompromised patients.
optionExplanations.c: Coccidioidomycosis causes valley fever in deserts of the southwest USA and northwest Mexico.
optionExplanations.d: PJP produces a non-productive cough with bilateral symmetrical interstitial infiltrates, not a lobar infiltrate with broad-based budding yeast.
optionExplanations.e: Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast acquired from soil contaminated with pigeon droppings and typically disseminates to the CNS in immunocompromised hosts.

questions.question: A 39-year-old man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 40 cells/mm3 presents with two weeks of headache, fever, and confusion. Lumbar puncture shows a raised opening pressure, and the CSF cryptococcal antigen test is positive. Culture is pending. What is the most appropriate initial antimicrobial therapy?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that in patients with HIV who have cryptococcal meningitis or severe pulmonary disease, amphotericin B (plus flucytosine) is used in the first 2 wk for induction therapy, followed by fluconazole for at least 8 wk as consolidation therapy and then a lower maintenance dose. Serial lumbar puncture or another method of managing increased ICP is an important adjunct, which this man needs given his raised opening pressure.

optionExplanations.b: Fluconazole is the consolidation and maintenance agent after induction, not initial therapy for cryptococcal meningitis.
optionExplanations.c: TMP/SMX is the preferred therapy for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, not cryptococcal disease.
optionExplanations.d: IV pentamidine is second line for severe PJP.
optionExplanations.e: Clotrimazole troches treat mild oral thrush.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man returns from three weeks in rural sub-Saharan Africa, where he took no antimalarial prophylaxis. He has four days of paroxysms of high spiking fever and shaking chills lasting several hours, headache, myalgias, and diarrhea. He has hepatosplenomegaly. Bloodwork shows thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, and anemia without leukocytosis. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Thick and thin blood smears with Giemsa stain, repeated every 12-24 hours
Rapid antigen detection test as the sole diagnostic test
Serologic antibody testing for Plasmodium species

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that malaria is investigated with microscopy using blood smears every 12-24 h (three sets) to rule out infection: a thick smear with Giemsa stain detects the presence of organisms and a thin smear with Giemsa stain allows species identification and quantification of parasites. This man has the classic paroxysms of high spiking fever and shaking chills with the CBC triad of thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, and anemia after travel to an endemic region.

optionExplanations.b: Rapid antigen detection tests are adjuncts; they do not identify the species or quantify parasitemia, which guides treatment of severe disease.
optionExplanations.c: Blood cultures do not grow Plasmodium species.
optionExplanations.d: Stool examination addresses intestinal parasites, not the erythrocytic infection responsible for these paroxysms.
optionExplanations.e: Serology does not distinguish current from past infection and is not the diagnostic test for acute malaria.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with 12 hours of fever, rigors, vomiting, and altered mental status. Blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg. She underwent splenectomy after a motor vehicle collision two years ago, takes no medications, and has had no recent chemotherapy or hospitalization. Blood cultures are drawn before antibiotics. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies asplenia and splenectomy as defects of humoral immunity, which make patients vulnerable to encapsulated organisms including S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, and GBS. This woman is asplenic and presents with fulminant sepsis, so an encapsulated organism is the expected pathogen.

optionExplanations.b: Staphylococcus is listed among the catalase-producing organisms that infect patients with defects of neutrophil function, such as chemotherapy or chronic granulomatous disease.
optionExplanations.c: Aspergillus is a catalase-producing organism seen with defects of neutrophil function, and is also a cause of fungal superinfection in prolonged neutropenia.
optionExplanations.d: Nocardia is also a catalase-producing organism associated with impaired neutrophil function, not asplenia.
optionExplanations.e: Candida is described as a fungal superinfection in prolonged neutropenia or with concurrent antibiotic use, not a consequence of splenectomy.

source.reference: ID44 — Infections in the Immunocompromised Host

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman is on day 10 of chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia. She develops a temperature of 38.6degC. Her absolute neutrophil count is 0.2. The exit site of her indwelling central venous catheter is erythematous and tender. She is normotensive, tolerating oral intake, and her chest x-ray is normal. What is the most appropriate empiric antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Oral antibiotics at home with next-day follow-up

questions.explanation: This is febrile neutropenia, defined as fever with an ANC below 1.0 (severe if below 0.5). Toronto Notes classifies patients who do not meet all the low-risk criteria as high risk, treated with IV monotherapy such as piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, imipenem, or meropenem, with vancomycin IV added for catheter-related infection, MRSA, severe mucositis, or previous quinolone prophylaxis. Her tender catheter exit site is a catheter-related infection, so vancomycin is added.

optionExplanations.b: Monotherapy is the backbone, but the catheter-related infection is a specific indication to add vancomycin.
optionExplanations.c: Vancomycin alone leaves Gram-negative organisms uncovered; high-risk febrile neutropenia requires broad-spectrum IV monotherapy as the backbone.
optionExplanations.d: Empiric antifungal therapy such as amphotericin B is considered if fever persists through day 3-5 or fungal infection is suspected or proven.
optionExplanations.e: Home oral antibiotics apply only to low-risk patients with a solid tumour, no comorbidities, and neutropenia expected to last under 10 d.

questions.question: A 71-year-old woman with recurrent urinary infections is admitted with fever, rigors, and right flank pain, and requires fluid resuscitation. Urine and blood cultures grow E. coli producing an extended-spectrum B-lactamase. She has no penicillin hypersensitivity and normal renal function. Which antibiotic is the most appropriate definitive therapy?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists the carbapenems imipenem, meropenem, and ertapenem as covering GN organisms including Enterobacter and extended-spectrum B-lactamase producers plus anaerobes, with a stated indication of infections caused by GNB producing extended-spectrum B-lactamases. Cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, and cefazolin are inactivated by these enzymes, and only newer combinations such as ceftolozane-tazobactam and ceftazidime-avibactam are listed for resistant GN infections, so meropenem is the correct choice here.

optionExplanations.b: Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin whose activity is lost to extended-spectrum beta-lactamases.
optionExplanations.c: Cefazolin is a first-generation cephalosporin with limited Gram-negative coverage, used mainly for skin and soft tissue infections and surgical prophylaxis.
optionExplanations.d: Cefuroxime is a second-generation agent used for respiratory and soft tissue infections and is not reliable against ESBL producers.
optionExplanations.e: Beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations are not the recommended treatment for ESBL producers, for which carbapenems or newer agents such as ceftolozane-tazobactam and ceftazidime-avibactam are used.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents with 3 d of painful spasms of the masseters and difficulty opening his mouth, 10 d after a deep puncture wound from a rusty nail. He has no record of immunization. Painful muscle spasms are triggered by loud noises, and he now has rigidity of the neck and abdomen, diaphoresis, and tachycardia. Which antimicrobial therapy is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes gives IV metronidazole as the antimicrobial therapy for generalized tetanus (IV penicillin G is listed as an effective alternative), alongside wound debridement, tetanus immune globulin to neutralize unbound toxin, and supportive care. Trismus with painful muscle spasms triggered by sensory stimuli, descending rigidity of neck and abdomen, and autonomic hyperactivity after traumatic implantation of spores in an unimmunized patient is clinically diagnostic of Clostridium tetani infection. Note that antimicrobial therapy may fail unless adequate wound debridement is also performed.

optionExplanations.b: Vancomycin is not the agent the source names for C. tetani, which is an anaerobic gram-positive bacillus treated with metronidazole.
optionExplanations.c: Ceftriaxone is not listed as therapy for tetanus; it does not address toxin-producing C. tetani in a devitalized wound.
optionExplanations.d: IV acyclovir is given empirically until herpes simplex encephalitis is ruled out, a different CNS presentation with fever and altered level of consciousness rather than trismus and tetany.
optionExplanations.e: Azithromycin has no role in tetanus; the source specifies metronidazole, with penicillin G as the alternative.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man returns to Canada after two years of agricultural work along fast-flowing rivers in sub-Saharan Africa, where he was bitten repeatedly by blackflies. Over the past year he has developed intensely itchy dermatitis and progressively worsening vision, now with near-blindness in one eye. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists ivermectin plus doxycycline as the management of Onchocerca volvulus, a nematode of sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America transmitted by blackfly bite and presenting with river blindness (onchocerciasis) and dermatitis. The blackfly exposure along river valleys combined with pruritic dermatitis and progressive visual loss identifies onchocerciasis rather than another roundworm.

optionExplanations.b: Diethylcarbamazine plus doxycycline is the listed management of Wuchereria bancrofti, a mosquito-borne filaria causing lymphedema and lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis), not dermatitis with blindness.
optionExplanations.a: Mebendazole is used for Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, and Enterobius vermicularis, intestinal nematodes acquired by ingestion of eggs rather than by blackfly bite.
optionExplanations.d: Albendazole is listed for intestinal nematodes and for Strongyloides stercoralis and Loa loa, but not as the treatment for onchocerciasis.
optionExplanations.e: Pyrantel pamoate is an option for Ascaris lumbricoides and for pinworm in pregnancy; it does not treat filarial infection.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with long-standing asthma and multiple environmental allergies has three months of worsening dyspnea, cough, and episodes of high fever. Serial chest radiographs show transient pulmonary infiltrates that change location, with no cavitation. Serum IgE is markedly elevated and sputum culture grows Aspergillus fumigatus. Her neutrophil count is normal and she is not immunosuppressed. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes gives the treatment of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis as corticosteroids plus itraconazole. ABPA is an IgE-mediated asthma-type reaction with dyspnea, high fever, and transient pulmonary infiltrates that occurs more frequently in patients with asthma and allergies, which is exactly this presentation. Voriconazole and amphotericin B are reserved for invasive aspergillosis, which is associated with prolonged and persistent neutropenia or transplantation rather than an immunocompetent asthmatic.

optionExplanations.b: Voriconazole is the treatment for invasive aspergillosis, which occurs with prolonged and persistent neutropenia or transplantation and causes severe fever, cough, dyspnea, and cavitation.
optionExplanations.c: Amphotericin B is the alternative to voriconazole for invasive aspergillosis, not for the IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction seen here.
optionExplanations.d: Fluconazole is listed for candidal infection, including chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and other systemic Candida infections, not for Aspergillus.
optionExplanations.e: Echinocandins are options for opportunistic Candida infections in HIV and other systemic candidal infections; they are not the treatment of ABPA.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man has six months of painless hematuria. A year ago he swam repeatedly in fresh water lakes in sub-Saharan Africa and developed a pruritic rash on his legs shortly afterwards. Ultrasound of the bladder shows a thickened, irregular wall with dilatation of the distal ureters. His complete blood count shows eosinophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Schistosome larvae (cercariae) penetrate unbroken skin during fresh water exposure and produce a pruritic rash at the site of penetration, called swimmer's itch or cercarial dermatitis. In S. haematobium the adult worms live in the vesical plexus and the eggs deposited in the distal ureter and bladder induce granulomas and fibrosis, causing hematuria and obstructive uropathy. The sub-Saharan fresh water exposure, eosinophilia, and bladder and ureteric findings therefore point to S. haematobium rather than the species that lodge in mesenteric veins.

optionExplanations.b: S. mansoni worms sit in the mesenteric vein with eggs in the portal tracts of liver and bowel, producing intestinal polyps, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly rather than bladder disease.
optionExplanations.c: Clonorchis sinensis is acquired from raw fish in Japan, Taiwan, China, and Southeast Asia and lives in the bile ducts, causing inflammation and sometimes cholangiocarcinoma.
optionExplanations.d: Echinococcus granulosus is acquired from dog feces in rural sheep-raising countries and causes slowly enlarging liver and lung cysts that may cause mass effect or rupture.
optionExplanations.e: Taenia solium cysticercosis follows ingestion of eggs in human feces and produces mass lesions in the CNS, eyes, and skin with seizures, not obstructive urinary disease.
